title: Martian Gambit: White's attack against 8...Bf7 and 8...Bf5
outcomes: Names the squares for the attacked bishop on g6 and what each gives White (a target, a tempo, a queen route)
Explains why 9.Bc4 develops first against 8...Bf7 and why a knight on f6 closes the g4 route
Finds the checkable refutation of 9...Nbd7 (the capture on f7 first, then the queen to g4) and sees that the queen-first order fails
Explains the pawn push against 8...Bf5 and why the retreat to h7 leaves e6 without a defender
Checks, before a queen move, whether a black piece attacks the landing square and whether the queen would be defended there

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** With the white knight on e5, the bishop has to leave g6. Which squares are real, and what does each one give White: a target, a tempo, a path for the queen? By the end you can name White's best set-up against each of the two main retreats, and the natural Black moves that lose. steps.text: **Same piece, two jobs.** On f7 the bishop stays close to the king and keeps the knight's attack in sight. On f5 it is active, and it also guards the e6 pawn, but a pawn push can drive it away. [I] Either way e6 is the pawn to watch: it stands alone with a hole behind it, and White's pieces will point at it.

Attacks with the queen come later, once the other pieces stand ready and the squares she needs are not covered.

steps.text: **8...Bf5: the bishop that can be chased.** On f5 the bishop develops and defends e6, but a pawn on g2 is one push from attacking it. White also has other tries, such as the bishop to c4 or a queen check. Your job in this chapter is to see which White move makes the bishop move away from its defensive post, and why that helps White.

steps.text: **What the routes teach.** [I] Against ...Bf7 White develops first and waits for a queen route to open. Against ...Bf5 White uses a pawn to chase the bishop away from e6. The common idea: attack the single defender of e6, then use the pawn as the target. Before a queen move, check whether a black piece attacks the landing square and whether the queen would be defended there.

steps.text: **Recap: what to remember.** The bishop must leave g6, and e6 is the target either way. Against ...Bf7, White develops the bishop first. Against ...Bf5, a pawn push chases the bishop and leaves e6 unguarded. The queen needs a landing square that no black piece attacks (or one she can defend), so a knight on f6 shuts the g4 route. Attacking the intruder with the b8 knight loses to a capture on f7 first.
